cl_mdma_peeing.q: Why is it hard to pee on MDMA?
cl_mdma_peeing.short: Nobody knows: no study has measured it. A water-holding hormone rose in 8 men on MDMA. Three studies with a dummy pill found no rise in it or its marker.
cl_mdma_peeing.but: None of these studies reported anything about pee. So nobody knows if the hormone has anything to do with it.
how: In 8 healthy men, the body's water-holding hormone rose 1 to 2 hours after one MDMA capsule. Only 3 of them also had a day without MDMA, and the study didn't test the difference.
In three studies, the same people took MDMA on one day and a dummy pill on another (16, 12 and 32 people). The hormone, or a marker released with it, didn't rise.

Blood salt fell a little after MDMA, and more when people drank a lot of water at once. The team that found this collected urine too, but never reported what it found. Low blood salt has its own answer.

The only case of someone who couldn't pee at all: a 19-year-old man, for 24 hours, after saying he'd taken 15 tablets in 36 hours. A tube drained his bladder. Nobody tested him or the pills for drugs.
cl_mdma_peeing.rate: One case report with no drug test, plus lab studies that measured a hormone and blood salt but not peeing. And their hormone results disagree.

cl_opi_conditioned_tolerance.q: Can using in a new place make an overdose more likely?
cl_opi_conditioned_tolerance.short: Maybe, but it's untested in people. In rats, a big dose killed 64 in 100 in a room not linked with heroin, and 32 in 100 in the heroin room.
cl_opi_conditioned_tolerance.but: The rats knew both rooms, so it wasn't a new place. In people, there's just one study: 10 survivors' memories, with nobody to compare.
how: The idea: the place, people and ritual that come with a drug start to trigger the body's push-back against it. That push-back is part of tolerance. So it may be weaker where the drug isn't usually taken.

In the rat study, each rat had heroin in one room and dummy injections of sugar water in the other. A big dose then killed about 64 in 100 rats in the dummy room, 32 in 100 in the heroin room, and 96 in 100 rats that had never had heroin.
Nobody measured the rats' tolerance, only whether they died. The paper also overstated how sure its result was, though more rats died in the dummy room in all six repeats. Rats aren't people.

In people, 10 overdose survivors were asked what was different that day. 7 recalled something unusual: 3 a new place or crowd, 2 a different way of injecting, 2 a different mix of drugs. Nobody counted how often people use somewhere new with no overdose.
cl_opi_conditioned_tolerance.rate: One tiny study of 10 people's memories, with nobody to compare them with, plus one rat experiment that compared two familiar rooms. Rat findings don't show what happens in people.

mdma.statement: Scientists have measured how MDMA affects peeing.
mdma.why: No study has. They measured a water-holding hormone and blood salt instead, and the one team that collected urine never reported what it found.

mdma.statement: All the studies found that MDMA raises the hormone that holds in water.
mdma.why: Not all: it rose in one small study of 8 men, but three studies with a dummy pill found no rise in it or its marker. None of them reported anything about pee.

heroin.statement: In the rat study, heroin was deadlier in a room the rats had never seen.
heroin.why: Every rat knew both rooms. Heroin killed about 64 in 100 rats in the room linked with dummy injections, against 32 in 100 in the room linked with heroin. Rats aren't people.

general.statement: It's been shown in people that a new place makes overdose more likely.
general.why: In people there's only one study: 10 overdose survivors' memories, with nobody to compare them with. And in the rat study, both rooms were familiar to the rats.
